definition: All the people who will live in the future, taken together.
example: The town buried a time capsule so that posterity would know how its residents lived.
nuance: Unlike descendants, which usually means one family's offspring, posterity usually means all future people, and it never means wealth, as prosperity does.
prompt: A scientist decides to record her field notes in careful detail.
options: She wrote clearly so that posterity could check her findings long after she retired.
She hoped the notes would bring her posterity in the form of a large salary.
She studied posterity to learn how scientists a century ago had worked.
Her posterity, the lab assistant sitting beside her, read each page as she finished it.
reasons: Readers who come generations later are exactly the audience the word names.
This mixes up the word with prosperity; a salary is money, not future people.
Scientists of a century ago belong to the past, but the word points forward in time.
A coworker in the room today is not a future generation, and one person is not a whole group.

practice.prompt: A city council debates whether to protect an old forest.
options: The mayor promised that selling the timber would bring the town instant posterity.
The council hoped to finish the vote in posterity, well before the meeting ended later tonight.
Members argued that the trees should be saved for posterity, not cut for quick profit.
The council traced its posterity back to the settlers who first cleared the land.
reasons: Instant riches would be prosperity; the word refers to people of the future, not money.
Later tonight is only hours away, while the word refers to generations far in the future.
Protecting the forest for people not yet born fits the word's focus on later generations.
Early settlers are ancestors; tracing back in time reverses the word's direction.
